texts.label: A
texts.title: Bike workshop at the Old Depot

paragraphs.text: Bike workshop at the Old Depot — drop-in sessions. Every Tuesday from 5 pm to 8 pm and every second Sunday from 10 am to 1 pm you may bring a bicycle and use our stands, tools and the help of a mechanic. There is no charge and no booking; arrive early on Sundays, as we take the last bike in at 12.15 so that everybody finishes before we close.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: You do the work and we show you how. We do not repair bicycles for people, partly because we could not keep up and mainly because the point of the session is that you can do it again at home. Parts are not free: common items — cables, brake blocks, tubes, chains — are sold at what they cost us, and anything we do not stock you buy yourself and bring. We cannot work on electric bicycles because of the battery, and we do not touch anything that is under a shop warranty.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Children are welcome with an adult, and a child may use the tools under the adult’s eye rather than ours. The room is upstairs and there is no lift, so anybody who cannot carry a bicycle up should telephone first and we will arrange to meet them in the yard. Bicycles may not be left overnight in any circumstances; a machine left after closing goes to the police as found property, which is a nuisance for everybody and has happened three times this year.
paragraphs.label: C

texts.label: B
texts.title: Warm space at St Alban’s Hall

paragraphs.text: Warm space at St Alban’s Hall, November to March. The hall is open Monday, Wednesday and Friday from 10 am to 3 pm to anybody who would like to sit somewhere warm. There is tea, coffee and soup at midday, all free and with no questions asked; nobody is signed in and nobody is asked why they have come. The hall is heated to twenty degrees, there are armchairs and tables, and the wifi password is on the wall.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: What else happens here depends on the day. A nurse holds a blood pressure check on Wednesdays from 11 am, a volunteer helps with forms and letters on Mondays, and on Fridays there is a repair table for small electrical items and clothing. None of these requires an appointment and all of them are used by people who came in for the heating and stayed for the conversation, which is what the scheme is for.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: We ask three things. Please do not bring alcohol into the hall; please tell a volunteer if you are unwell rather than sitting quietly with it; and please take a cup back to the hatch when you have finished, because the same six people wash up every week. Donations of tea, coffee, tinned soup and warm socks are welcome and are left in the box by the door. If you want to help, come on a Monday at half past nine and ask for the coordinator.
paragraphs.label: C

texts.label: C
texts.title: Lone working: what the policy requires

paragraphs.text: Lone working: what the policy requires. A lone worker is anybody working out of sight and sound of a colleague, which includes a driver, a night cleaner, an engineer in a plant room and a member of staff who stays late in an otherwise empty office. The policy applies to all of them equally, and the first requirement is simple: your manager knows where you are and when you expect to finish.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Before a task is done alone it is assessed, and the assessment is written rather than remembered. It asks three questions: could this task go wrong in a way that would leave somebody unable to call for help; is there a safer way to do it at a time when others are present; and what would happen if the person did not return. A task that fails the first question is not done alone, whatever the inconvenience, and nobody is asked to make that judgement on their own initiative in the middle of a shift.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Contact is arranged in advance and is checked both ways. You tell the duty office when you arrive and when you leave; if a check-in is missed, the office telephones, and if there is no answer within fifteen minutes it sends somebody. Staff working in areas without a signal carry a device that works over the satellite network, and the device is tested at the start of each shift rather than trusted because it worked yesterday.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Some things are never done alone, and the list is short and absolute: work at height above three metres, entry into a confined space, work on live electrical equipment, and any task requiring breathing apparatus. A supervisor who authorises one of these for a lone worker is in breach of the policy regardless of the outcome, and an employee who is asked to do one may refuse without any consequence, which is written here so that it can be pointed at.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Handling customer information. Every employee who can see customer records completes the data course before being given access and repeats it every two years. The rule that covers most situations is that you look at a record because you need it for the task in front of you, and not for any other reason; curiosity about a neighbour, a celebrity or a former partner is the commonest cause of dismissal in this area, and every access is logged with your name against it.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Information is given out only to the customer, and only when identity has been confirmed by the standard questions. A person who says they are calling on behalf of a customer is told what the customer must do to authorise that, rather than being given anything; the exception is an account with a registered representative, which shows on the record. Never confirm that somebody is a customer to a caller who does not already know, because that is itself information.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Records are not taken off the premises. Do not photograph a screen, do not email a file to a personal address in order to finish at home, and do not carry printouts in a bag; where work at home is agreed, it is done through the company system, which keeps everything on the server. A document that has to be destroyed goes into the confidential bin and not the ordinary one, and a full confidential bin is reported rather than propped open.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: If information goes where it should not, report it within the hour to the data manager, whatever the day or time. Most breaches are small and ordinary — an email to the wrong address, a letter in the wrong envelope — and the damage depends almost entirely on how fast they are noticed and acted on. Nobody has been disciplined for reporting their own mistake quickly; several people have been disciplined for hoping that nobody would notice.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: A place name looks like the most stable thing on a map and is among the least. Names are changed by conquest, by administration, by fashion and by simple error, and the version printed today is a snapshot of an argument rather than a fact about the ground. Most towns of any age have been called several things, and the one in use is frequently the version that a clerk wrote down at a moment when writing it down mattered.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Many names began as descriptions and stopped being understood. A settlement called something that once meant the ford by the ash trees keeps the sound long after the trees and the ford have gone and after the language that named them has been replaced; speakers then hear the syllables as a name rather than as words. This is why place names are among the best evidence for languages that left almost no other trace, and why the study of them belongs to linguistics as much as to history.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Errors are preserved with the same care as anything else. A surveyor mishears a local word, a printer drops a letter, a clerk copies the entry above by mistake, and the result becomes official because it is written in the official book; correcting it later requires more effort than living with it. Several well-known names are the result of a foreign visitor asking a question and recording an answer that meant something quite different, which is a story told about more places than it can be true of.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Administrative renaming is the most deliberate kind and the most argued about. A new government renames streets, towns and sometimes a whole region to mark that something has changed, and the change is real in law and partial in practice: the old name survives in speech, in the name of a station, in the way older people give directions, and often returns when the government that made the change has gone. Studies of such renamings find that the ones that last are those that replaced a name nobody had an attachment to.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Two names for one place is the ordinary condition rather than the exception. A city may have one name in the language of the country and another in the language of a neighbour or a former ruler; a mountain may have a name used by the people who live under it and another that appears in international lists. The interesting question is not which is correct but which is used by whom, and a mapping service that has to choose learns quickly that there is no neutral answer.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Restoration of older names has become common and is not always simple. Where a name was imposed and the earlier one is remembered, returning to it is straightforward and popular; where the earlier name is known only from documents, or where several communities remember different earlier names, the restoration itself becomes a choice between claims. Some countries have handled this by recognising two names officially, printing both on signs and accepting that people will use one.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Names also disappear without anybody deciding. Field names, the names of individual trees, of bends in a river and of parts of a village are held by the people who use them daily and vanish within a generation when the work that used them stops; a farm sold to somebody from elsewhere takes its field names with the last person who needed them. Volunteer projects that record such names before they go are among the few pieces of local history that cannot be done later.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What the subject teaches is a kind of caution. A name carries a claim about who was here, what they did and what language they did it in, and the confidence of a printed label conceals how much of that is guesswork, borrowing and accident. Reading an old map with that in mind is a better exercise in historical method than most textbooks manage, and it can be done with the map of the district anybody happens to live in.
paragraphs.label: H

topic.en: Three sections: a bike workshop and a winter warm space, lone working and customer data, and an essay on why place names change.
